name: Hair texture powder / sea salt spray
lead: Texture powders and sea salt sprays are hair styling products used to make hair look fuller, grippier and more tousled, with a matte, lived-in finish rather than a shiny, slicked one. Sea salt spray is a salt-and-water mist applied to damp hair to encourage waves and body, while texture powder is a fine dry powder dusted at the roots to add lift and hold [1][3][4].

Wikipedia's article on styling products explains that volumisers add temporary volume, body and shine to thin or flat hair, with humectants swelling the strand and polymers coating it, and that mousse can add texture for a beach-blown effect [1]. A dedicated Wikipedia article on hair texture powder describes modern formulas as lightweight powders, often based on silica or rice starch, that add body and separation without a sticky or stiff feel, in volumising, matte and texturising variants [4]. No clinical studies of either product were found.

For people with thinning or fine hair, these products are a cosmetic way to look like they have more density at the front and crown. On looksmax.org, members share homemade sea salt sprays and discuss them for adding waviness and curl [3].

paras: General styling products work by coating strands with polymers, wax or oil, or by swelling the strand with humectants [1]. Volumisers are described as products that add temporary volume and body to thin or flat hair, available as shampoo, conditioner, spray, pomade or lotion, and are typically applied to damp roots and blow-dried [1]. Sea salt sprays and texture powders sit in that wider category; their formulations vary by brand.

Mousse, a lighter foam than gel, can add volume and shine and is also used to define curls or create a beach-blown texture on damp hair [1]. Sea salt spray is the more direct version of that beach look, a liquid applied to damp hair and left to dry, often finished by scrunching or blow-drying, which is how forum users describe using it [3].

Texture powders are dry formulas shaken or dusted onto the roots and mid-lengths. According to Wikipedia, they are popular for adding root volume, which suits fine or thinning hair, and for giving hold and definition without the stiffness of hair spray or gel. Volumising powders lift the roots, matte powders reduce shine, and texturising powders add grit for a tousled look [4].

They are related to dry shampoo, a powder product usually sold in aerosol cans whose starch absorbs scalp oil; Wikipedia notes dry shampoo can also add volume, help tease hair and substitute for mousse [5]. Wikipedia lists possible side effects of dry shampoo, including follicle inflammation, dermatitis and residue build-up, and the oil and powder stay on the scalp until a wash [5].

Powder in the hair is far older than modern styling products. Powdered starch or flour was used on wigs and natural hair as early as the late 1500s and early 1600s, hair powder was a status symbol among the upper classes in France and England in the 18th century, and its use declined after the French Revolution as natural styles came into fashion and taxes were placed on it [4].

Modern styling products have their own chronology: Chase Products first packaged hair spray in the US in 1948, hair spray became the best-selling beauty product on the market by 1964, and the 1980s punk movement popularised gel for spiky styles [1][6]. Hair gel and waxy styling agents are traced to the ancient Egyptians and Gauls [1][7].

For people who are growing out their hair or have fine or thinning hair, texture products are a low-commitment way to change how the hairstyle reads in photos and in person: adding lift at the crown, separating strands and removing shine. They are also used with wavy or curly hair to emphasise the pattern.

One looksmax.org thread presents a homemade version of sea salt spray, using water, salt and a little olive oil in a spray bottle, applied to hair after washing and scrunched in to encourage curl [3]. The author reports tighter curls afterwards, while another user replies that the hair was already curly [3].

Wikipedia notes that most styling products do not damage hair when applied properly, but any product can dry hair, and some ingredients can strip oils or build up and cause dullness, dryness, breakage, eczema or thinning [1]. Conditioning overviews describe heat, bleaching and weathering as separate sources of damage that strip the cuticle's lipid layer [2]. Aerosol powders and dry shampoos carry flammability and inhalation considerations noted for the category [5].

lore.intro: Sea salt spray appears in hair-texture threads, including a do-it-yourself recipe presented as a cheaper alternative to commercial sprays [3].

claims.claim: A homemade sea salt spray can make hair wavier or curlier.
claims.believers: The poster reports that his wavy hair became tighter curly after using it, while a replier says the hair was already curly. [3]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested sea salt sprays for curl formation; reference sources on styling products do not describe them. [1]

claims.claim: Texture powder makes thinning or fine hair look fuller
claims.believers: Users and product descriptions present root powders as a way to add volume at the crown and hairline [4].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes texture powders as popular for adding root volume on fine or thinning hair [4]. No published studies have measured perceived density with these products.

claims.claim: Powder is a lighter alternative to gel or spray
claims.believers: Advocates describe powders as giving hold without stiffness or stickiness [4].
claims.experts: Wikipedia contrasts hair spray, which can feel crunchy unless brushed out, and gel, which has stronger hold, with lighter-feeling powders [1][4].

card.summary: Salt mist and dry powder for matte, voluminous hair; cosmetic styling with no clinical research.
card.aka: Sea salt spray, texturizing powder, volumizing powder
card.note: Styling products can dry hair or build up (per Wikipedia).

quick.overview:
Sea salt spray and texture powder are styling products meant to give hair volume, grip and a matte look. Sea salt spray is applied wet and powder is dusted dry.
Users share DIY sea salt sprays online. No clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Styling products generally coat or swell the hair strand to create temporary body.
quick.risks: Styling products can dry hair or build up and cause dullness or breakage, according to Wikipedia. No specific safety studies on these two product types were found.

chain: Apply salt mist to damp hair or dust powder at the roots
Strands are coated or roughened, adding grip and lift
angle.text: Sea salt spray and texture powder change how hair sits for the day, adding volume, grip and a matte tousled finish. Users apply them to make styles hold and thin hair appear fuller until the next wash.
